result.text: The paper addresses the overlooked opportunity in multi-task recommendation systems to transfer task-specific predictive knowledge (e.g., click vs. purchase signals) across tasks to improve overall performance. The key insight is that per-task prediction outputs encode fine-grained, transferable preferences that, if properly aligned and distilled, can serve as supervision for other tasks without causing harmful task conflicts. The proposed Cross-Task Knowledge Distillation framework creates auxiliary tasks with quadruplet ranking losses to capture cross-task relations, uses a calibrated distillation scheme to align disparate output magnitudes before transferring knowledge, and introduces an error-correction mechanism that enables synchronous teacher–student training; experiments on real datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.

The paper addresses the challenge that Transformers must store local and global information within the same element-wise representations and struggle with long sequences due to self-attention’s quadratic cost. The key insight is that adding a separate, trainable memory that is passed recurrently between fixed-size segments lets the model decouple local token representations from global state and propagate long-range information without changing core Transformer operations. Methodologically, the authors implement memory as special tokens appended to input or output segments, train the Transformer to read, write and maintain these memory tokens across segments (yielding a segment-level recurrent Transformer), and show that this Recurrent Memory Transformer matches Transformer-XL on language modeling with small memory and outperforms it on longer-range tasks, while also improving Transformer-XL when memory tokens are added.

The paper addresses the vulnerability that machine unlearning systems—designed to efficiently remove a user’s data from trained models instead of retraining from scratch—can be forced to incur the full retraining cost, undermining practical guarantees and denial-of-service resistance. Its key insight is that certification formalisms for unlearning often ignore computational budgets, creating an attack surface where carefully crafted training examples (poisoning points) can be made pivotal so that any subsequent removal request for them forces the unlearning mechanism to fall back to expensive retraining. The authors formalize this attack objective, construct poisoning strategies that maximize the likelihood a point becomes influential enough to trigger retraining under common certified unlearning schemes, and empirically validate on standard datasets that small, targeted perturbations in training data substantially increase the rate of full retraining events, thereby demonstrating a realistic and efficient denial-of-service vector against certified machine unlearning.

The paper tackles the problem of estimating a trained classifier’s accuracy on unlabeled test sets from changing environments where obtaining labels is costly. The key insight is that semantic classification accuracy and the self-supervised rotation-prediction accuracy, when trained jointly, exhibit a strong linear relationship (Pearson r > 0.88) across various datasets and test conditions. The method trains a model to perform both semantic classification and rotation prediction, measures rotation accuracy on unlabeled test images (because rotation labels are free to generate), and then uses simple linear regression calibrated on labeled validation data to predict the classifier’s semantic accuracy on new unlabeled test sets.

The paper addresses the lack of large-scale, egocentric datasets that combine accurate 3D camera geometry with annotated video understanding for neural rendering and dynamic scene modeling. Its key insight is that augmenting an existing action-rich egocentric video corpus (EPIC-KITCHENS) with reconstructed camera poses and geometry removes the costly photogrammetry bottleneck and better supports tasks that require both spatial structure and semantic labels. The authors introduce EPIC Fields, a dataset that registers 19M frames across 45 kitchens (recovering cameras for 96% of videos) and pairs these 3D-enabled videos with action segments and VISOR object masks, and they demonstrate the utility by proposing methods and strong baselines for neural rendering and dynamic object segmentation that reveal current limitations and show geometry improves semi-supervised segmentation.

The paper addresses how to learn effective state representations for reinforcement learning, particularly for robotic object-manipulation tasks, by leveraging 3D scene understanding; existing learned or hand-engineered low-dimensional states can be insufficient for complex visual observations. The key insight is that supervising an encoder with a latent-conditioned Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) forces the latent space to capture object geometry and appearance across multiple views, producing a representation better aligned with downstream control needs. The method trains an encoder to map multiple camera images into a latent code while a NeRF decoder reconstructs images from that code, using the NeRF reconstruction loss as supervision, and then uses the learned latent as the RL agent’s state input (NeRF-RL), showing improved performance on tasks like hanging mugs, pushing, and opening doors.

The paper addresses exploration-exploitation in finite-horizon reinforcement learning when the state-action space has a metric structure and potentially high-dimensional, continuous aspects. The key insight is that one can exploit smoothness of the MDP by using nonparametric kernel smoothing to estimate rewards and transition dynamics and combine those estimates with optimism to guide exploration, yielding strong sample-efficiency without strong parametric assumptions. The authors propose Kernel-UCBVI, a model-based optimistic algorithm that builds kernel-based estimates of rewards and transitions, constructs confidence sets via kernel-UCB-style uncertainty quantification, and plans optimistically within those sets; they prove a finite-time regret bound of Õ(H^3 K^{2d/(2d+1)}) where d is the covering dimension of the joint state-action space, and validate the method empirically on continuous MDPs with sparse rewards.

The paper challenges the common assumption that vision architectures require a locality inductive bias by showing that vanilla Transformers treating each individual pixel as a token can perform competitively across multiple vision tasks. The key insight is that per-pixel tokenization—eschewing the 16×16 patch aggregation used in Vision Transformers—still allows the model to learn effective image representations for supervised classification/regression, masked autoencoding self-supervision, and diffusion-based image generation. Methodologically, the authors simply apply standard Transformer architectures to sequences of pixel tokens (with appropriate positional embeddings and comparable training setups) and compare performance to patch-based counterparts, demonstrating surprisingly strong results despite higher computational cost. This finding suggests that locality priors like patching are not strictly necessary for high performance, prompting reconsideration of architectural biases in future vision models.

The paper addresses negative transfer in diffusion-based generative models by reframing diffusion denoising at different noise levels as a multi-task learning (MTL) problem and showing that tasks with widely separated noise levels have low affinity and can conflict, degrading performance. The key insight is that negative transfer in diffusion training can be mitigated by grouping similar denoising tasks so MTL techniques operate on smaller, coherent subsets rather than across all timesteps, and that timesteps naturally form contiguous intervals of compatible tasks. Methodologically, the authors cluster denoising tasks into interval-based clusters (using objectives built from signal-to-noise ratio, timestep, and task affinity and solved efficiently via dynamic programming) and apply existing MTL loss/gradient-modulation methods within each cluster, yielding better generation quality and faster convergence while keeping computation tractable.

The paper tackles amodal segmentation, specifically the problem of predicting occluded object regions without being misled by background or occluders, which existing methods often do by using whole-image features. Its key insight is that amodal completion should rely primarily on the visible region together with learned shape priors—mirroring human perception—so that predictions are invariant to different occluders given the same visible parts. The proposed method first predicts coarse visible and amodal masks, then refines the amodal mask by focusing feature extraction on the visible region and retrieving category-specific shape priors from a memory/codebook to guide completion, thereby suppressing background/occluder signals and producing more robust, interpretable amodal masks. Evaluation on three datasets shows state-of-the-art performance and visualizations demonstrate that the learned codebook entries capture meaningful category-specific shape information.

Experiments on ZJU-MoCap and AIST demonstrate substantial improvements over recent generalizable NeRF approaches for novel humans and poses.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of machine learning models against data poisoning attacks that modify, delete, or insert training examples. The key insight is that bagging’s subsampling and majority-vote structure provides intrinsic, algorithm-agnostic resilience: if the number of poisoned training points is below a derived threshold, the ensemble’s majority vote cannot be flipped regardless of the base learner’s behavior. result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

result.text: The paper tackles decision-making in MDPs where chosen actions are executed only after an m-step delay—a realistic but challenging setting where naive state-augmentation scales exponentially and ignoring delays can cause failures. The key insight is that optimal performance can still be achieved using Markov policies defined on the original state space, provided these policies are allowed to be non-stationary across the delay horizon, whereas stationary Markov policies are generally suboptimal. Building on this, the authors derive theoretical results about the sufficiency of non-stationary Markov policies and introduce a model-based, non-stationary Q-learning style algorithm that avoids state-augmentation; empirically it converges rapidly and outperforms or rescues learning in tabular, physics-based, and Atari tasks with substantial delays.

The paper addresses the quadratic computation and memory bottleneck of self-attention in vision transformers, which limits scalability to long token sequences for visual recognition. The key insight is that keeping the softmax normalization in attention prevents effective linearization, so removing softmax and replacing the scaled dot-product with a Gaussian kernel allows the full attention matrix to be approximated as a low-rank factorization. The method, called SOFT, uses Gaussian-kernel-based similarity without further normalization and computes a robust low-rank approximation by estimating the Moore–Penrose inverse via a Newton–Raphson procedure, yielding linear complexity in tokens. Experiments on ImageNet show SOFT achieves much better computational efficiency and enables much longer token sequences while maintaining or improving accuracy compared to prior ViT variants.

The paper tackles the scalability limits of autoregressive transformers for very long, tokenization-free sequences (e.g., raw bytes for images, audio, and long text), where standard self-attention is quadratic and impractical. The key insight is to factor modeling into local, within-patch submodels and a lighter global model between patches so the model can capture fine-grained byte structure locally while sharing context globally, enabling sub-quadratic attention and larger per-token feedforward capacity for the same compute. Megabyte implements this as a multiscale decoder that segments input into patches, applies dense local transformers to model intra-patch dependencies, and uses a sparser global transformer to propagate inter-patch context, which also improves parallel decoding. result.text: The paper addresses the vulnerability that machine unlearning systems—designed to efficiently remove a user’s data from trained models instead of retraining from scratch—can be forced to incur the full retraining cost, undermining practical guarantees and denial-of-service resistance. Its key insight is that certification formalisms for unlearning often ignore computational budgets, creating an attack surface where carefully crafted training examples (poisoning points) can be made pivotal so that any subsequent removal request for them forces the unlearning mechanism to fall back to expensive retraining. The authors formalize this attack objective, construct poisoning strategies that maximize the likelihood a point becomes influential enough to trigger retraining under common certified unlearning schemes, and empirically validate on standard datasets that small, targeted perturbations in training data substantially increase the rate of full retraining events, thereby demonstrating a realistic and efficient denial-of-service vector against certified machine unlearning.

The key insight is that negative transfer arises not only from optimization-level gradient interference but also from poor auxiliary-to-target generalization, so dynamically selecting and combining task contributions based on target validation performance better prevents harmful updates. result.text: The paper tackles continual learning when a stream of tasks can be a mix of similar (transferable) and dissimilar (unrelated) tasks, a setting where prior methods only handle one or the other and either suffer catastrophic forgetting or miss opportunities for transfer. The key insight is to treat each incoming task adaptively: detect whether it is similar to any previous tasks and, if so, selectively transfer relevant knowledge from those tasks, whereas if it is dissimilar prioritize mechanisms that prevent forgetting. The proposed method implements this by automatically detecting task similarity and then applying different update rules within a single network—selective knowledge transfer for similar tasks and forgetting-mitigation strategies for dissimilar ones—allowing both forward and backward transfer as well as retention. Empirical results on mixed-task sequences show the approach improves new-task learning when transfer is possible while still protecting past-task performance when tasks are unrelated.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of obtaining sharp regret guarantees for the Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (GP-UCB) algorithm in kernelized bandits, where prior analyses gave suboptimal (sometimes non-sublinear) rates for common kernels like Matérn. The key insight is that tighter regret bounds follow from regularizing the kernel ridge regression estimator proportionally to the kernel’s smoothness and leveraging a concentration inequality in separable Hilbert spaces that had been largely overlooked. Methodologically, the authors reanalyze GP-UCB by introducing smoothness-proportional regularization and combining it with the Hilbert-space concentration result to control estimation error more tightly, which yields nearly optimal, sublinear regret rates for Matérn and related kernels and thus resolves a longstanding open question.

The paper addresses the limited granularity of existing visual transformers, which split images into relatively large patches and thus may miss fine-scale, within-patch structure important for recognizing objects at different scales and locations. Its key insight is that modeling attention not only between coarse patches (sentences) but also inside each patch among smaller subpatches (words) yields richer representations with little extra cost. The proposed Transformer in Transformer (TNT) embeds each large patch as a sequence of smaller patch tokens, applies an inner transformer to compute “word” attention within each patch and an outer transformer to model “sentence” attention across patches, and aggregates word- and sentence-level features end-to-end. Experiments on ImageNet and other benchmarks show TNT improves accuracy (e.g., +1.7% top-1 over similar-cost visual transformers) while maintaining comparable computational complexity.

args.text: We propose a bilevel affinity-guided training scheme for diffusion models that jointly learns timestep clusters, curricula, and routing. Starting from contiguous timestep clusters initialized by SNR/affinity, we learn per-cluster curricula that prioritize harder (low-noise) steps while a lightweight routing module allocates more task-specific channels to early timesteps; within each cluster, RotoGrad-style gradient rotation and normalization reduce residual conflicts. The outer loop updates cluster memberships and curriculum weights using differentiable proxies of difficulty/relatedness (e.g., relative-entropy shifts between adjacent noising distributions), allowing clusters to merge/split as training progresses. This unifies optimization, architecture, and scheduling to mitigate negative transfer, improving convergence and sample quality without inference-time overhead.

result.text: The paper tackles improving contrastive learning by introducing feature-level augmentations, specifically for graphs (and images), to complement common input-space augmentations and better leverage less dominant features. The key insight is that subtracting a low-rank approximation from each feature map—obtained via a novel "incomplete power iteration"—rebalances the spectrum and injects controlled noise into singular values, which emphasizes smaller singular components without perturbing singular vectors and thus improves alignment between views. Methodologically, they compute a low-rank estimate per feature map with one or two iterations of this incomplete power iteration, form the residual (complement) as the augmented feature, and align rebalanced feature maps across views; they derive closed-form analyses of the spectral-balancing effect and variance introduced, prove improved generalization bounds, and empirically show better performance and compatibility with other augmentations and contrastive losses.

result.text: This paper tackles sample-efficient exploration in model-based reinforcement learning by designing and analyzing posterior sampling algorithms that achieve strong regret and sample-complexity guarantees. args.text: We propose Batchwise Affinity Meta-Routing (BAMR) for diffusion training: instead of fixed global timestep intervals, BAMR builds a minibatch-specific affinity graph over timesteps using SNR and gradient cosine similarity, then partitions it into small neighborhoods on-the-fly. Each neighborhood shares lightweight DTR-style channel gating and small adapter parameters, while distant timesteps are decoupled to reduce interference and allocate extra capacity where early, coarse denoising needs it. To mitigate residual negative transfer and automatically schedule learning, we meta-learn per-neighborhood loss weights and gradient rotations via short-horizon hypergradients on a held-out anchor-timestep validation loss, unifying curriculum, routing, and principled MTL alignment. The result is dynamic, example-conditioned clusters that can split or merge during training, improving convergence and sample quality while remaining compatible with standard diffusion design-space improvements.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation that standard Transformers distinguish tokens only by a single token-level position index, which may underutilize hierarchical textual structure and thus constrain contextual representations for language modeling and understanding. The key insight is that richer positional signals—explicit, combined encodings for paragraph, sentence, and token segments—can make attention more segment-aware and improve both autoregressive and masked-language pretraining. Methodologically, the authors integrate a segment-aware combined position encoding into Transformer-XL (yielding Segatron) and into BERT pretraining (SegaBERT), retaining relative position and memory mechanisms while augmenting inputs with paragraph/sentence token indices; this yields lower perplexity on WikiText-103 and improved downstream and zero-shot sentence-representation performance compared with baseline Transformers.

The paper tackles the gap between practical “unlearning” procedures and true data-deletion privacy in machine learning, showing that existing unlearning guarantees are insufficient because (a) deletion requests that depend on published models induce interdependence among records so retraining alone may not protect deleted users, and (b) caching partial computations across releases can leak deleted information over time. The key insight is that protecting deleted records requires ensuring the privacy of the remaining records as well—privacy of existing data is necessary for privacy of deletions—and that sound deletion guarantees must account for adaptive deletion behavior and cumulative leakage. Building on this, the authors formalize a robust deletion notion and introduce a secure, accurate, and computationally efficient unlearning procedure based on noisy (differentially private) gradient descent that avoids reusable cached state and adds calibrated noise to gradients to prevent long-term leakage while maintaining model utility.

args.text: We propose an online, object-centric 4D radiance memory for egocentric video that fuses calibrated camera geometry from EPIC Fields with VISOR masks to incrementally build per-object dynamic NeRFs during daily activities. The memory is updated from sparsely sampled frames modulated by IMU-derived head-motion cues (as in EgoDistill) and uses decoupled object-agnostic vs. object-specific feature propagation to gate reliable updates, preserving identity through long occlusions and out-of-frame intervals. args.text: We propose Multi-Proxy Accuracy Identification (MPAI) to estimate a trained classifier’s target-domain accuracy without labels even when label marginals shift or a novel class appears. Jointly train the classifier with a suite of self-supervised proxies (e.g., rotation, jigsaw, masked prediction) and, on source/validation splits, fit a hierarchical linear model mapping class-conditional proxy accuracies to semantic accuracies; at test time, combine observed proxy scores with an estimated target label distribution (and optional open-set mass) to solve for per-class and overall accuracies via a constrained least-squares system. Residual structure across proxies flags open-set mass and yields calibrated lower bounds when a novel class absorbs unexplained variance. Learning proxy weights further stabilizes the estimator, turning proxy–accuracy correlations into an identifiable system robust to relaxed/open-set label shift.

args.text: I propose Hierarchical Latent Recurrent Memory: a training-free long-context wrapper that inserts a small, fixed-size latent memory array between merge stages of a chunked transformer. Each layer first processes local chunks and reduces tokens, then cross-attends to and updates a shared latent memory (Perceiver-style) that is carried recurrently across layers and across successive segments like memory tokens; at inference, we initialize or augment this memory via approximate kNN over a library of past latent memories from related documents to import relevant global state. This decouples global context propagation from token representations, keeps compute sublinear via hierarchical merging, and enables persistent cross-document recall without finetuning. We hypothesize substantial gains on needle-in-haystack and multi-hop long-range QA at million-token scales while preserving the base model’s weights.

args.text: Visible-slot-conditioned diffusion for amodal instance segmentation (VSDAIS). We train a latent diffusion model to complete amodal masks conditioned on the RGB crop, the detected visible mask, and an object-centric slot embedding; the slot encodes category-agnostic shape priors and is optionally augmented by retrieved expansion prototypes that steer the denoising trajectory. Synthetic occlusion layering and depth-ordered training enforce occluder invariance, while sampling multiple completions yields calibrated uncertainty and enables robust consensus masks; for videos, flow-conditioned slots impose temporal consistency. This unifies visible-region-focused amodal completion, prior-guided expansion, object-centric slot modeling, and discrete diffusion-based mask generation, addressing brittleness to occluders and improving generalization.

result.text: We propose GoalKD-MoE, a goal-conditioned cross-task distillation framework for recommender RL that transfers dense behavioral signals (e.g., clicks, dwell) to sparse, high-value goals (e.g., purchases) without negative interference. Building on a GoalRec-style world model, we learn goal-conditioned trajectory embeddings and universal value heads, then distill predictions across goals with calibrated scale alignment and per-example transfer weights derived from a learned representation-based task distance (as in TAWT). To balance sharing and isolation, action/value networks are organized as a differentiable k-select Mixture-of-Experts whose gate is trained jointly with the distillation to route states toward experts that benefit a given source-to-target goal pair. This yields a single policy/value system that adaptively decides when and how much to transfer across goals, improving sample efficiency and stability on multi-metric recommendation benchmarks.

result.text: The paper studies machine unlearning—removing a subset of training data's influence from a trained model—by asking which properties of the forget set make unlearning hard and how algorithms behave on non-random deletion requests. The key insight is that unlearning difficulty is driven by interpretable characteristics of the forget set (e.g., homogeneity, influence, or representativeness) and that evaluating algorithms on forget sets that isolate these factors exposes failure modes invisible with random deletions. The authors propose RUM (Refined-Unlearning Meta-algorithm): split the forget set into homogeneous subsets based on those characteristics, apply existing unlearning methods to each subset, and combine the results to produce a model that better satisfies forgetting while preserving utility. Empirically, RUM substantially improves top-performing unlearning algorithms and provides a principled framework for diagnosing and addressing unlearning challenges.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised monocular depth estimation in dynamic scenes by explicitly modeling per-object 6-DoF motion together with camera ego-motion, addressing failures of prior methods that treat moving objects as outliers. Its key insight is that correctly handling object motion requires a geometrically accurate forward-projection formulation (not the common inverse projection) and that combining instance-aware photometric and geometric consistency yields stronger self-supervision for both background and object regions. The method implements a neural forward-projection module to render objects under estimated 6-DoF transforms, integrates a unified instance-aware consistency loss that enforces photometric and geometric alignment for each segmented instance, and leverages an auto-annotation pipeline using off-the-shelf instance segmentation and optical flow to produce video instance masks for training. Empirically, this end-to-end framework improves depth and motion estimation on KITTI and Cityscapes, outperforming prior state-of-the-art approaches.

args.text: We propose Action-Conditioned Object Radiance Fields (AC-ORF) for visual RL: unsupervised object-centric 3D decomposition produces per-object radiance fields that serve as the agent’s state, and a lightweight action-conditioned dynamics head predicts how each object’s latent field transforms under executed action sequences. Training jointly maximizes mutual information between (current object-ORF latents, action sequence) and future ORF latents via a temporal action-driven contrastive objective, while a light-field rendering head provides fast multi-view supervision and A-LIX-style encoder gradient constraints stabilize TD learning. Compared to NeRF-supervised state learning, AC-ORF targets control-sufficient, occlusion-robust, and compositional states that support transfer from few-object tasks to many-object settings. A two-stage self-expert cloning pretrain with strong augmentations can further endow radiance latents with visual invariances before RL fine-tuning, improving zero-shot robustness to appearance shifts.

args.text: We propose Diversity-Aware Diffusion Training (DADT), which brings formal task-diversity theory to the denoising-timestep view of diffusion models. We estimate a per-timestep diversity profile using tractable proxies (e.g., Fisher–Rao distance or relative-entropy between consecutive noising distributions and score outputs), then (i) partition timesteps into the smallest intervals whose within-cluster diversity stays below a threshold and (ii) allocate minibatch sampling probabilities proportional to each timestep’s marginal “representation gain” (diversity × gradient-variance). This yields clusters and curricula that are data-driven rather than hand-tuned and come with sample-complexity intuition: when inter-cluster diversity is high, the shared representation within each cluster is identifiable, improving convergence and reducing negative transfer. Practically, DADT plugs into existing clustered/curriculum diffusion training and routing modules and consistently speeds training and improves FID/IS without inference-time cost.

result.text: The paper addresses the overlooked opportunity in multi-task recommendation systems to transfer task-specific predictive knowledge (e.g., click vs. purchase signals) across tasks to improve overall performance. The key insight is that per-task prediction outputs encode fine-grained, transferable preferences that, if properly aligned and distilled, can serve as supervision for other tasks without causing harmful task conflicts. The proposed Cross-Task Knowledge Distillation framework creates auxiliary tasks with quadruplet ranking losses to capture cross-task relations, uses a calibrated distillation scheme to align disparate output magnitudes before transferring knowledge, and introduces an error-correction mechanism that enables synchronous teacher–student training; experiments on real datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.

result.text: We propose Diversity-Aware Diffusion Training (DADT), which brings formal task-diversity theory to the denoising-timestep view of diffusion models. We estimate a per-timestep diversity profile using tractable proxies (e.g., Fisher–Rao distance or relative-entropy between consecutive noising distributions and score outputs), then (i) partition timesteps into the smallest intervals whose within-cluster diversity stays below a threshold and (ii) allocate minibatch sampling probabilities proportional to each timestep’s marginal “representation gain” (diversity × gradient-variance). This yields clusters and curricula that are data-driven rather than hand-tuned and come with sample-complexity intuition: when inter-cluster diversity is high, the shared representation within each cluster is identifiable, improving convergence and reducing negative transfer. Practically, DADT plugs into existing clustered/curriculum diffusion training and routing modules and consistently speeds training and improves FID/IS without inference-time cost.

result.text: The paper tackles the ambiguity about which denoising timesteps are harder when training diffusion generative models and how that affects learning and convergence. The key insight is that earlier (lower) timesteps are empirically more difficult—exhibiting slower convergence and larger relative-entropy shifts between consecutive distributions—so organizing training from easier to harder tasks can aid learning. Methodologically, the authors cluster timesteps or noise levels by difficulty and apply a curriculum learning schedule that trains models in ascending difficulty rather than jointly across all timesteps, yielding faster convergence and improved image-generation performance across unconditional, class-conditional, and text-to-image settings while remaining compatible with other diffusion training improvements.

Its key insight is to represent a scene as depth-ordered object-centric layers and to use a transformer-like architecture that ingests optical flow so that each learned query corresponds to an object-layer for the entire video, enabling object permanence and temporal shape consistency. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of machine unlearning—efficiently and accurately removing specific training samples to satisfy data-erasure requests (e.g., GDPR) without degrading model performance. Its key insight is that forgetting can be achieved quickly and precisely by targeting layer-level representations, especially the final layer, and combining targeted sample identification with soft-label transfer to preserve decision boundaries. The method first uses a Partial-PGD algorithm to efficiently locate samples to forget, then performs unlearning confined to the last layer inspired by Forward-Forward, and finally applies knowledge distillation from the original model as a teacher so the updated model retains accuracy via soft labels. Experiments comparing to state-of-the-art unlearning methods show this layer-attack unlearning is both faster and more accurate in end-to-end unlearning performance.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of domain adaptation when the target domain exhibits relaxed label shift—i.e., changes in label marginals possibly alongside changes in class-conditionals—which existing benchmarks and methods do not systematically evaluate, leaving many heuristics vulnerable to degraded performance. Its key insight is that many popular domain-adaptation heuristics fail under substantial label-proportion shifts, but a simple, broadly compatible two-step correction—pseudo-balancing training data each epoch and then adjusting the final classifier using an estimate of the target label distribution—can substantially recover accuracy. The authors introduce RLSbench, a large-scale benchmark of over 500 shift pairs across vision, tabular, and language tasks with varying label proportions, use it to evaluate 13 methods revealing widespread failures, and show that their meta-algorithm improves accuracy by typically 2–10 points under large shifts while minimally affecting performance when proportions do not shift.

args.text: We propose a streaming egocentric 3D scene memory that distills NeRF-like volumetric features from sparsely sampled frames fused with head IMU, avoiding dense per-frame computation. The model is pretrained in simulation to hallucinate occluded local layout and persistent surroundings, then finetuned on EPIC Fields with recovered camera poses to anchor geometry in real videos; during training and online updates we apply hand-inpainting to factor out agent occlusions while preserving grasp cues. This memory supports long-horizon object re-detection by projecting and querying persistent 3D features, which we hypothesize will improve egocentric long-term tracking and reasoning on benchmarks like EgoTracks. Training uses teacher–student feature distillation from a heavyweight video backbone, IMU-conditioned pose-consistency, and cross-view projection consistency.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised inference of object-centric, 3D scene representations from a single image—i.e., learning to decompose a scene into objects and backgrounds in a way that explains image formation and supports 3D reasoning—without any manual annotations. The key insight is to marry neural radiance field (NeRF)-style differentiable 3D scene representation and volumetric rendering with amortized deep inference networks so the model can learn object radiance fields (ORFs) and a compositional rendering process directly from multi-view RGB data. Their method, uORF, trains an encoder that maps a single image to latent object codes and scene parameters and a decoder that instantiates per-object radiance fields and a learned compositing/rendering pipeline; the whole system is trained end-to-end with view-consistency losses, enabling unsupervised discovery, segmentation, novel-view synthesis, and 3D editing.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing when function approximation enables provable, polynomial-sample reinforcement learning across diverse MDP models. Its key insight is that many previously studied models (and new ones like the Linear Q*/V* model) can be unified under a Bilinear Classes structural condition that reduces RL generalization to a supervised learning problem, allowing sample complexity to be expressed in terms of supervised generalization error. args.text: We propose Dynamic Spectral Token Routing for ViTs: at selected layers, features are transformed to the frequency domain (per-window or globally), and a tiny policy head predicts a content-adaptive mask over frequency bins to keep, guided by energy and task-gradient saliency. Retained bins are inverted to a compact set of spatial tokens that receive full self-attention, while pruned bins are propagated via cheap linear spectral updates and can be selectively reintroduced in deeper layers through cross-scale synthesis. Training uses differentiable hard masking with FLOP-budget regularization and an aliasing-aware guard band to avoid artifacts when pruning high frequencies. This bridges spatial token pruning/merging with FFT-based global mixing, concentrating attention on semantically informative spectra while preserving low-frequency global context, yielding large savings on high-resolution dense tasks.

result.text: Visible-slot-conditioned diffusion for amodal instance segmentation (VSDAIS). We train a latent diffusion model to complete amodal masks conditioned on the RGB crop, the detected visible mask, and an object-centric slot embedding; the slot encodes category-agnostic shape priors and is optionally augmented by retrieved expansion prototypes that steer the denoising trajectory. Synthetic occlusion layering and depth-ordered training enforce occluder invariance, while sampling multiple completions yields calibrated uncertainty and enables robust consensus masks; for videos, flow-conditioned slots impose temporal consistency. This unifies visible-region-focused amodal completion, prior-guided expansion, object-centric slot modeling, and discrete diffusion-based mask generation, addressing brittleness to occluders and improving generalization.

result.text: The paper tackles learning interactive recommender systems from logged user feedback without any opportunity for online exploration, aiming to maximize cumulative user rewards despite distributional mismatch between logging and target policies. Its key insight is to cast recommendation as a probabilistic generative model and perform offline stochastic policy inference, combined with multiple principled mechanisms to constrain or correct for the gap between the logging policy and the learned policy. The method develops an inference algorithm for discrete stochastic policies from logged data and introduces five complementary strategies—support constraints, supervised regularization, explicit policy constraints, dual constraints, and reward extrapolation—to reduce distributional shift during offline training. Experiments on two public real-world datasets show these techniques yield better cumulative-reward performance than standard supervised and prior offline RL approaches for recommendation.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of extending pre-trained LLMs to handle very long input contexts without costly retraining or prohibitive self-attention memory use. The key insight is that long-context processing can be achieved training-free by hierarchically merging local chunk representations across transformer layers, using token reduction before each merge so that computation and memory grow much more slowly with input length. The method, called HOMER, divides inputs into chunks, processes them in parallel, then iteratively merges adjacent chunks at progressively higher layers with a lightweight token-reduction step and an optimized merge ordering that reduces peak memory to logarithmic scaling in sequence length; experiments show this yields better long-context understanding and markedly improved memory efficiency.

result.text: The paper tackles domain adaptation when the target label marginal can change arbitrarily and may include a previously unseen class—a setting called Open Set Label Shift (OSLS)—while assuming class-conditional distributions p(x|y) are invariant across domains. The key insight is that, under this invariance, the problem of simultaneously estimating the shifted target label distribution (including a novel class) and learning a target classifier becomes identifiable and therefore amenable to principled methods, subsuming both label-shift and positive–unlabeled learning as special cases. Practically, the authors derive necessary and sufficient identifiability conditions and propose algorithms that leverage black-box predictors to estimate the target label proportions and train classifiers, providing theoretical finite-sample and Gaussian-linear convergence guarantees and demonstrating 10–25% accuracy gains over open-set domain-adaptation baselines across vision, language, and medical benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the limitation of egocentric video understanding methods that rely on short clip-level visual features and therefore fail to capture the camera-wearer’s broader, persistent environment and unseen local surroundings. The key insight is that training models to predict and encode the latent, human-centric environment from first-person video—using simulated 3D environments where full observability provides supervisory signal—yields environment-aware representations that transfer to real-world egocentric footage. The method trains on videos of agents in simulated scenes to learn features predictive of the local, potentially occluded environment and then plugs those learned representations into downstream human-centric video tasks; this yields consistent improvements over clip-only features and, despite simulation-only training, strong performance on real-world datasets including state-of-the-art results on the Ego4D NLQ challenge.

args.text: We propose Graph-NeRF Control: a perception module amortizes a 3D, per-object radiance-field slot decomposition from egocentric video and aggregates slots into a spatial interaction graph on which a goal-conditioned policy operates, enabling combinatorial generalization to variable numbers of objects. We train perception and dynamics with an action-driven contrastive objective that maximizes mutual information between (current graph + action sequence) and future object-slot states, aligning latents with control, while a NeRF-style reconstruction loss enforces multi-view consistency. To improve zero-shot robustness, we decouple policy learning and invariance acquisition via a self-expert cloning stage that transfers behavior from weak to strongly augmented views in graph space. This unifies entity-centric control, object-centric dynamics modeling, and 3D-aware representation learning to scale multi-object manipulation and withstand large visual shifts.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency of vision transformers by recognizing that final predictions depend on a small subset of informative tokens, so processing all tokens throughout the network is wasteful. The key insight is to dynamically and progressively prune redundant tokens per input using a lightweight importance-prediction module inserted at multiple layers, exploiting self-attention so that removed tokens can be masked out without harming differentiable training or hardware efficiency. Concretely, the method trains tiny token-scoring heads end-to-end with an attention-masking strategy that blocks pruned tokens’ interactions, hierarchically sparsifies up to ~66% of tokens, and thereby reduces FLOPs and increases throughput with minimal accuracy loss, producing competitive complexity/accuracy trade-offs on ImageNet.

result.text: The paper tackles the gap between diffusion models and multi-task learning by explicitly designing architectures that route task-specific information across the denoising timesteps. Its key insight is that denoising at different timesteps behaves like related tasks with strong local affinity—adjacent timesteps should share channels while earlier timesteps need more task-specific capacity to recover global structure—so selectively activating subsets of channels (sliding-window affinities and timestep-weighted capacities) can better match architecture to task dynamics. The method, Denoising Task Routing (DTR), is a lightweight add-on that gates channels per timestep according to a sliding affinity pattern and allocates more task-specific channels for early (coarse) timesteps, requiring no extra parameters; this routing improves sample quality, speeds convergence, and complements MTL optimization techniques, enabling smaller models to match larger-model performance with far fewer training iterations.

Methodologically, GoalRec learns a high-capacity, reward-independent world model to simulate user dynamics under given goals and uses those predictions to train the disentangled universal value function, thereby reducing variance and improving generalization; experiments on simulations and a real application show improved handling of the three identified challenges.

result.text: The paper addresses the high memory cost of KV caching during generative inference with large language models by proposing a plug-and-play way to compress the KV cache without retraining. The key insight is that attention heads exhibit distinct, predictable structures—some focus on local context, some on special tokens, and some attend broadly—so the cache can be adapted per-head to keep only the vectors that matter. The method profiles attention patterns cheaply, then constructs an adaptive KV cache that evicts long-range entries on local-focused heads, drops non-special tokens on special-token-focused heads, and retains full caches for globally attending heads; this profiling-guided FastGen approach reduces GPU memory use substantially while preserving generation quality and requires no expensive fine-tuning.

result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of ballooning Key-Value (KV) cache size and the resulting memory/time costs when LLMs process very long contexts. The key insight is that individual attention heads consistently attend to a small set of prompt positions and that this head-specific attention pattern can be predicted from a short “observation” window at the end of the prompt. SnapKV leverages this by clustering and selecting the important KV positions per head (without finetuning) and only storing those compressed KV entries during generation, yielding similar accuracy while keeping decoding latency stable and dramatically reducing memory use. Empirically, SnapKV speeds decoding ~3.6×, improves memory efficiency ~8.2× on 16K inputs, scales to ~380K tokens on a single A100 with negligible accuracy loss, and maintains baseline performance across 16 long-context datasets.

args.text: We propose accuracy forecasting under distribution shift via a bank of self-supervised probes and label-shift-aware calibration. Concretely, we train a shared encoder with multiple cheap probes (e.g., rotation, patch permutation, blur/frequency prediction) whose accuracies respond differently to class-conditional vs marginal changes, and learn a small meta-learner that maps the probe-accuracy vector plus estimated target label proportions to predicted semantic accuracy using a few labeled environments for calibration. At test time, we estimate target label proportions (including novel-class mass) with an open-set label-shift estimator, compute probe accuracies on the unlabeled target, and output both a point estimate and conformal prediction interval; large residuals act as an open-set alarm. result.text: The paper tackles efficient compression of Transformer models for resource-constrained deployment, noting that prior weight-focused low-rank approximations perform poorly for transformers and require large labeled datasets to fine-tune. Its key insight is that activations (features) in transformer layers are empirically low-rank even though the learned weight matrices are not, so compressing outputs rather than weights yields more faithful reduction. Building on this, the authors introduce AAFM, which adaptively determines per-layer compression structure and locally compresses each linear layer's output features in a few-shot, unsupervised manner, followed by a global fine-tuning stage GFM that holistically optimizes the compressed network; both stages use only a small unlabeled sample set. The method achieves substantial parameter and latency reductions with minimal accuracy loss (e.g., 33% parameters removed and 18.8% throughput gain with only 0.23% ImageNet accuracy drop using 2K unlabeled images), transfers to NLP tasks, and generalizes well to downstream tasks.

The paper addresses exploration-exploitation in finite-horizon reinforcement learning when the state-action space has a metric structure and potentially high-dimensional, continuous aspects. The key insight is that one can exploit smoothness of the MDP by using nonparametric kernel smoothing to estimate rewards and transition dynamics and combine those estimates with optimism to guide exploration, yielding strong sample-efficiency without strong parametric assumptions. The authors propose Kernel-UCBVI, a model-based optimistic algorithm that builds kernel-based estimates of rewards and transitions, constructs confidence sets via kernel-UCB-style uncertainty quantification, and plans optimistically within those sets; they prove a finite-time regret bound of Õ(H^3 K^{2d/(2d+1)}) where d is the covering dimension of the joint state-action space, and validate the method empirically on continuous MDPs with sparse rewards.

args.text: We propose PyramidKV, a training-free multi-scale KV cache for long-context LLM inference that combines hierarchical token reduction with head-specific routing. During prefill, each head builds a KV pyramid: full-resolution slots at the base, progressively pooled chunk summaries at higher levels (via lightweight token-reduction akin to hierarchical merging/pooling), and a tiny set of recurrent memory tokens for global state. At decode time, a per-head pattern predictor routes queries to the coarsest sufficient levels and triggers on-demand refinement to fine-grained KV only in selected regions, while evicting stale fine caches elsewhere; mixed-scale sparse kernels enable efficient lookup across levels. This yields near-logarithmic memory with stable latency and preserves accuracy by allocating precision where attention actually concentrates.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of machine learning models against data poisoning attacks that modify, delete, or insert training examples. The key insight is that bagging’s subsampling and majority-vote structure provides intrinsic, algorithm-agnostic resilience: if the number of poisoned training points is below a derived threshold, the ensemble’s majority vote cannot be flipped regardless of the base learner’s behavior. The authors prove a tight bound on that threshold (tight when no assumptions are made about the base learner), derive a certification procedure that counts how many base models’ training sets would be affected by a given tampering budget, and empirically validate the approach on MNIST and CIFAR-10—reporting, for example, 91.1% certified accuracy on MNIST against arbitrary modifications/deletions/insertions of 100 training examples.

The key insight is that token resolution should be dynamic per image: by starting with few coarse tokens and progressively refining only when needed, one can retain accuracy for difficult cases while saving computation on easy ones. The authors implement this as a cascaded Dynamic Transformer that sequentially activates Transformers with increasing token counts and stops inference early when confidence is sufficient, along with feature-reuse and relationship-reuse mechanisms to avoid redundant computation across stages. args.text: We propose ActOR-SE3: learning SE(3)-equivariant action operators over object-centric radiance fields for sample-efficient visual RL. Scenes are represented as per-object slots with radiance fields, while an action encoder maps continuous controls into Lie-algebra operators that transform object slots; training jointly maximizes action-conditioned predictive consistency between (state, action sequence) and future object states and enforces multi-view NeRF reconstruction after applying the induced operators. result.text: The paper addresses sequential control of unknown, possibly non-smooth nonlinear dynamical systems by learning dynamics modeled as an unknown function in a known Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space, which allows very general (including infinite-dimensional) system descriptions and both discrete and continuous controls. The key insight is that regret can be controlled not by the ambient state or parameter dimension but by information-theoretic quantities (mutual information / kernel complexity) derived from the RKHS prior, enabling exploration that is explicitly calibrated to uncertainty. The proposed Lower Confidence-based Continuous Control (LC^3) algorithm constructs lower-confidence-reactive controllers using posterior/GP-style uncertainty sets over dynamics and plans policies that trade off exploration and exploitation, and the analysis yields near-optimal O(√T) episodic regret bounds that depend only on information gain rather than dimensionality; experiments on nonlinear control tasks illustrate the practical benefit of this principled exploration.

args.text: We propose Anti-Aliased Token Subsampling (AATS) for ViTs: before any token pruning or merging, apply a content-adaptive low-pass prefilter aligned to the prospective sampling lattice to suppress high-frequency components that would otherwise alias when tokens are dropped. Using attention-derived spectral estimates, AATS instantiates lightweight depthwise or Fourier-domain filters to prefilter regions slated for reduction, while preserving a small set of explicitly tagged high-frequency “detail tokens” that are routed through the fast path. This plug-in augments existing token-reduction schemes (merging or pruning) and dynamic-resolution cascades, improving robustness and stability with negligible overhead and often fewer FLOPs due to cleaner downsampling. We hypothesize and test that anti-aliased subsampling yields better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs and OOD robustness, especially at high resolutions and early-stage reductions.

result.text: The paper addresses how to better compose and transfer knowledge from fine-tuned pre-trained models by exploiting structure within task vectors (the weight differences from pre-training) to improve multi-task composition, few-shot learning, and robustness to domain shift. The key insight is that parameter blocks of task vectors can be linearly combined with learned, block-specific coefficients to produce anisotropic scaling—only a few coefficients are needed because pre-trained models have low intrinsic dimensionality—so composition can be made more disentangled and less interfering. The proposed method, aTLAS, learns blockwise linear combination weights that scale task-vector components anisotropically, enabling selective mixing of the most informative parameter blocks across tasks and reducing data and memory requirements; experiments show it improves task arithmetic, few-shot recognition, and test-time adaptation under supervised and unsupervised objectives and scales as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach.

result.text: The paper tackles camouflaged object detection (COD), where objects blend into complex backgrounds causing ambiguous boundaries and overconfident wrong predictions. Its key insight is to reframe COD as a conditional mask-generation problem and use diffusion-based denoising to progressively refine segmentation while naturally producing diverse plausible masks, thereby reducing overconfident point estimates. The method, CamoDiffusion, conditions a diffusion model on the input image and designs specialized network architecture, loss/training strategies, and sampling schemes to boost expressive power and boundary refinement; stochastic sampling yields multiple candidate segmentations and the denoising process sharpens predictions, yielding state-of-the-art results on multiple COD benchmarks (notably COD10K with MAE 0.019).

result.text: The paper addresses catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) by providing the first theoretical analysis of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures in a CL setting. The key insight is that MoE can provably mitigate forgetting by diversifying experts to specialize on different tasks while a learned router selects and balances load across experts, but unlike standard (single-task or non-continual) MoE, the gating network must eventually stop updating to ensure convergence and bounded forgetting. Methodologically, the authors analyze overparameterized linear regression tasks to derive explicit formulas for expected forgetting and generalization error, show how expert specialization and router behavior reduce interference, characterize how more experts affect convergence speed (potentially harming performance if too many are added), and validate the theory with experiments on synthetic and real datasets and DNNs to inform practical MoE design for CL.

result.text: The paper tackles inefficient adaptation of large pretrained vision transformers to multiple dense vision tasks, where standard fine-tuning is costly and existing parameter-efficient techniques from NLP do not transfer well due to hierarchical vision architectures. The key insight is that task-specific adaptation for hierarchical vision transformers can be made both compact and effective by decomposing shared task information and applying lightweight, layer-aware modulation rather than naively attaching frozen adapters per task. To realize this, the authors introduce Polyhistor and Polyhistor-Lite, which combine Decomposed HyperNetworks that generate task-specific weights from a small set of shared parameters with Layer-wise Scaling Kernels that apply fine-grained, layer-adaptive scaling, enabling cross-task parameter sharing; experiments across four dense vision tasks show superior or competitive accuracy while using substantially fewer trainable parameters (about 10% of competing state-of-the-art), with larger gains for bigger models and more pretraining.

args.text: We propose budget-certified unlearning by coupling anti-pivotal training with subsampled ensembles: during training, add a max-influence regularizer that penalizes the per-example Fisher-preconditioned gradient/IJ norm to flatten the influence landscape, so no single point becomes pivotal. At deployment, train a small bagged ensemble with disjoint subsamples and, upon a deletion, apply one-shot total-Hessian Newton-style unlearning with Gaussian calibration per base learner; DP composition across deletions yields adaptive-sequence guarantees while the ensemble structure caps how many bases are affected by any forget set. This delivers a computable certificate that any k-point deletion requires at most a fixed budget B of unlearning steps (bounded by the subsampling overlap) and guarantees bounded prediction drift, simultaneously mitigating DoS-trigger deletions and unlearning-induced backdoors. We outline theory tying the budget B and drift bounds to the max-influence penalty, bagging overlap, and minimax sensitivity, and validate that APT maintains utility and deletion capacity while preventing forced-retraining events.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of large memory and computation costs from Key-Value (KV) caches in long-context language model inference and the limitations of prior token-dropping methods that irreversibly lose information. The key insight is that most attention heads attend only to local context while a small subset of "retrieval heads" attend broadly across the entire input, so preserving full histories only for those heads can retain necessary global information. Building on this, RazorAttention is a training-free compression algorithm that keeps a full KV cache for retrieval heads, prunes remote tokens for non-retrieval heads, and introduces a lightweight "compensation token" mechanism to recover information from dropped tokens. Evaluations on multiple large models show over 70% KV cache reduction with negligible performance loss, and the method is compatible with FlashAttention for efficient, plug-and-play deployment without retraining.

result.text: The paper tackles sample-inefficient Q-function learning in continuous state-action reinforcement learning under a generative model, where classical nonparametric rates scale exponentially in the joint dimension of states and actions. We propose Anti-Aliased Token Subsampling (AATS) for ViTs: before any token pruning or merging, apply a content-adaptive low-pass prefilter aligned to the prospective sampling lattice to suppress high-frequency components that would otherwise alias when tokens are dropped. result.text: The paper addresses the sample inefficiency of visual reinforcement learning, particularly the difficulty of learning control-relevant representations from pixels and the neglect of continuous action representation learning in prior self-supervised objectives. Its key insight is that jointly maximizing mutual information between latent encodings of current states paired with action sequences and encodings of the resulting future states forces the learned state and action latents to capture information sufficient for control. The proposed method, TACO, implements a temporal action-driven contrastive loss that simultaneously trains state and action encoders by contrasting positive (state+action sequence → future state) pairs against negatives, and integrates this loss into both online and offline RL pipelines; empirically it yields substantial sample-efficiency gains in online visual continuous control and improves offline visual RL performance across datasets.

result.text: The paper addresses how to adapt Masked Autoencoders (MAE) for self-supervised pre-training of irregular 3D point clouds to learn hierarchical, multi-scale representations that capture both local geometry and high-level semantics. The key insight is that pyramid (multi-scale) encoder–decoder architectures combined with a multi-scale masking scheme and local spatial attention better preserve and propagate spatial context across scales than flat transformers, enabling effective global-to-local reconstruction and transfer. Methodologically, Point-M2AE downsamples point tokens in a staged encoder with consistent visible regions across scales, applies multi-scale masking and local self-attention during fine-tuning, and uses a lightweight decoder that upsamples tokens with skip connections to reconstruct masked points progressively; this pre-training yields state-of-the-art linear and fine-tuned performance on multiple 3D benchmarks.

The paper addresses when and why representation-based transfer learning can reduce sample complexity for new tasks by learning a shared feature map from multiple related tasks. The key insight is that task diversity — a formal, general notion introduced by the authors — is the crucial property that lets a shared representation be identified from task-specific outputs, leading to a decomposition of sample complexity into representation and task-specific parts; with sufficiently diverse tasks, learning the shared representation from t tasks requires about C(H) + t C(F) samples while learning a new task using that representation requires only about C(F) samples. Methodologically, the authors formalize tasks as functions f_j ∘ h in a composite class F ∘ H, introduce a general diversity condition and prove statistical guarantees via a novel chain rule for Gaussian complexities, then instantiate the framework in several concrete models to demonstrate how the bounds apply.

result.text: The paper tackles offline preference-based reinforcement learning, where an agent must learn from fixed trajectory data and human pairwise preferences without online interaction or explicit reward functions. Its key insight is that learning a separate scalar reward is an unnecessary information bottleneck because dynamics and task information are orthogonal, so jointly modeling trajectories and preferences can directly recover task-consistent behavior. The proposed method, Offline Preference-guided Policy Optimization (OPPO), optimizes a contextual policy via an offline hindsight information matching objective while concurrently fitting a preference model to select optimal contexts, and iteratively refines the decision policy by alternating between these two objectives. Empirically, OPPO more accurately captures preferences and outperforms baselines that rely on learned or true rewards when applied with offline RL.

args.text: Most KV-cache compression methods either drop tokens or keep them per head, underutilizing that the aggregate contribution of dropped tokens to attention can be compactly approximated online. We propose SketchKV: a training-free, head-wise adaptive scheme that allocates per-head retention budgets via a bound-driven allocator, selects the retained KVs from a short observation window, and compresses all remaining KVs into a tiny, queryable linear sketch (e.g., softmax random-feature or value-weighted count-sketch) represented as a few "sketch tokens" appended to the cache. At decode time, each head attends over its retained KVs plus its sketch tokens, yielding near-baseline outputs while shrinking memory substantially; the sketch is updated in a streaming fashion and adapts when head patterns drift. This unifies head-structure profiling, bounded distortion, and compensation into a single plug-and-play mechanism compatible with fast attention kernels and without any fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses how to certify the collective robustness of general bagging ensembles against global data-poisoning attacks—i.e., how many test predictions can be simultaneously flipped when an attacker tampers with the training data. The key insight is that collective (global) robustness can be exactly characterized by computing the maximum number of changed predictions as a binary integer linear program (BILP), which enables tight certificates and reveals limits of vanilla bagging while suggesting structural changes to reduce influence scope of each poison. The method formulates and solves the BILP to certify worst-case simultaneous prediction changes, derives upper bounds on the poison budget tolerated by standard random-subsampling bagging, and introduces “hash bagging,” a deterministic, hash-based subsampling scheme that constrains which training points affect which base models to substantially improve certified robustness with little extra cost, validated by extensive experiments.

args.text: Leverage self-supervised auxiliary tasks as identifiable mixture fingerprints to jointly estimate target label proportions (including an unknown component) and predict unlabeled test accuracy under domain shift. Concretely, train a classifier with one or more auxiliary tasks (e.g., rotations), record per-class auxiliary-task accuracy signatures on a labeled validation split, and at test time solve a nonnegative mixture-matching problem to fit the observed auxiliary accuracies on unlabeled target data, yielding an estimate of the target label marginal (augmented with a meta-learned unknown-class signature) for label-shift correction and open-set handling. Then predict semantic accuracy from auxiliary accuracies via a calibrated linear model, but condition this mapping on the estimated label mixture so it remains valid under relaxed label shift. This unifies unsupervised performance monitoring with principled label-shift/OSLS estimation and can be evaluated on RLSbench and OSLS benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses offline preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL), where only pairwise trajectory preferences from humans are available instead of explicit rewards, and aims to provide provable learning guarantees with general function approximation. The key insight is to decouple reward inference and robust planning by first performing maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to recover an implicit trajectory-level reward model from offline preference data and then planning over a confidence set around this MLE to guard against estimation error, with coverage of the target policy characterized by a novel single-policy concentrability coefficient. Methodologically, the authors give polynomial-sample guarantees for recovering any target policy that is covered by the offline dataset (bounding this single-policy concentrability by the usual per-trajectory concentrability), prove matching lower bounds showing such concentrability is necessary and distinct from standard RL, and extend the framework and analysis to the case where preferences are provided over action pairs.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of machine unlearning for sequences of data deletions that are chosen adaptively in response to published models, a setting where prior non-convex unlearning methods only guarantee correctness for non-adaptive (independent) deletion sequences. The key insight is to reduce adaptive deletion guarantees to non-adaptive ones by leveraging differential privacy and its connection to max-information: a model-training procedure that is differentially private limits how much adaptive deletion choices can depend on published models, so non-adaptive unlearning bounds can be converted into adaptive ones. Concretely, the authors combine this reduction with existing non-adaptive unlearning techniques to produce general algorithms that provide provable deletion guarantees for arbitrary model classes and training methods, and they both theoretically show why earlier non-convex approaches fail under adaptive deletions and empirically demonstrate a practical attack that breaks the SISA algorithm on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST.

result.text: VISOR addresses the problem of accurate, temporally consistent pixel-level segmentation and hand–object relation annotation in long, egocentric videos where objects undergo transformative interactions (e.g., peeling, chopping, cooking) that break assumptions of existing video segmentation datasets. The key insight is that scalable, high-quality dense annotations for such complex, long-term interactions can be achieved by combining careful annotation protocols with AI-assisted tools to interpolate masks and maintain short- and long-term consistency across frames and object state changes. The authors build a large benchmark by annotating 36 hours of EPIC-KITCHENS footage with 272K manual semantic masks across 257 object classes, 9.9M interpolated dense masks, and 67K hand–object relations using a semi-automated pipeline, and they release three benchmark challenges focusing on video object segmentation, interaction understanding, and long-term reasoning along with data, code, and leaderboards.

The paper addresses the memory bottleneck caused by the KV cache during autoregressive inference of large language models, which can exceed model weight size and limit throughput due to constrained batch sizes. result.text: The paper addresses redundancy and inefficiency in multi-head attention within transformers, where many attention heads learn overlapping representations and inflate compute and parameter costs. args.text: We propose Active SSL Audit: estimate a classifier’s accuracy on unlabeled, shifted (and possibly open-set) targets by coupling self-supervised probe accuracies with mixture-identifiable label-shift modeling and label-efficient calibration. Co-train the classifier with rotation (and related) probes and learn on source a linear map from probe accuracies to per-class semantic accuracies; on a new target, infer shifted label proportions (including a novel class) via OSLS-style constraints and plug probe accuracies into the map to predict per-class and overall accuracy. Request a handful of target labels chosen by expected-gradnorm to fit a small domain-specific calibration that corrects residuals, and report diagnostics on RLSbench-style relaxed shifts. This unifies unlabeled accuracy estimation with principled open-set label-shift inference and theoretically grounded query selection.

I propose Adaptive Mixture-of-Keys KV Sketching: a training-free, head-wise KV compression scheme that maintains a small Gaussian mixture over each head’s key space and replaces dropped tokens with mixture centroids and mass-weighted value averages to approximate attention outputs. Concretely, we fit/update B per-head components online (streaming EM or k-means with covariance scaling); at decode time, we compute attention over these centroids (with cluster mass as a logit bias) instead of the full cache, while preserving exact entries for detected special-/retrieval-heads. Budgets B are allocated per head via a sensitivity-guided bound (à la adaptive eviction) and head selection is bootstrapped from a short observation window, yielding constant-memory tails with low distortion and compatibility with Flash/sparse kernels. This unifies head-aware eviction with MGK-style multi-region expressivity to deliver large KV reductions at similar quality, and should particularly excel on long-context prompts with clustered attention patterns.

args.text: We propose Hierarchical KV Summaries: a training-free, head-aware KV cache that replaces distant token-level KVs with a small set of per-head, chunk-level summaries built via HOMER-style hierarchical merging during prefill. For each merge, we form summary KVs by attention-pooling child tokens, keep only recent raw KVs in VRAM, and store an inverted index to top child tokens per summary on CPU. During generation, all heads attend over recent raw KVs plus summaries; if a summary receives high attention, we lazily expand it by fetching its top-k child KVs on demand, yielding near-constant latency and O(log n) long-range memory while avoiding irreversible drops. We build a video latent diffusion model that decodes depth-ordered object slots into frames, where each slot carries an amodal mask and appearance; conditioning on the RGB, per-frame visible masks, and diffusion-predicted flow/depth fields enforces occlusion-aware consistency across time. A lightweight discrete diffusion head refines the per-slot masks from the latent trajectory to yield sharp amodal segmentations with calibrated uncertainty, while synthetic occlusion layering and visible-region-focused priors guide completion away from occluders. Joint sampling across slots produces diverse but layer-consistent completions and a consensus estimator improves tracking and amodal IoU on occluded video benchmarks.

result.text: We propose GoalKD-MoE, a goal-conditioned cross-task distillation framework for recommender RL that transfers dense behavioral signals (e.g., clicks, dwell) to sparse, high-value goals (e.g., purchases) without negative interference. Building on a GoalRec-style world model, we learn goal-conditioned trajectory embeddings and universal value heads, then distill predictions across goals with calibrated scale alignment and per-example transfer weights derived from a learned representation-based task distance (as in TAWT). To balance sharing and isolation, action/value networks are organized as a differentiable k-select Mixture-of-Experts whose gate is trained jointly with the distillation to route states toward experts that benefit a given source-to-target goal pair. This yields a single policy/value system that adaptively decides when and how much to transfer across goals, improving sample efficiency and stability on multi-metric recommendation benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the often-overlooked privacy cost of hyperparameter tuning in differentially private learning, showing that choosing hyperparameters based on multiple training runs can leak sensitive information even if individual trainings are analyzed.
